editions.headline: Make review work visible before promising speed.
editions.summary: The useful career question is not how many screens AI can produce. It is whether a senior designer can make the decisions, review effort and missing expertise visible.

editions.headline: A migration is a product decision, not a library swap.
editions.summary: This week’s design-system and accessibility programs offer a useful senior-IC question: when teams modernize their tools, who owns the behavior customers must not lose?

editions.headline: A convincing demo is not a calmer product.
editions.summary: Fresh prototype examples and a conference session on calm design suggest a useful test: does the experience reduce the work people must supervise, or merely make automation look impressive?

editions.headline: Your design system needs a decision layer.
editions.summary: Fresh guidance makes design intent more usable by agents. The senior-design opportunity is to define where those instructions work, where they fail, and who can change them—not just to generate more screens.

editions.headline: An accessible feature still needs an accessible way in.
editions.summary: Discovery, control and ownership are design problems—not finishing touches. Three public event agendas offer a useful lens on senior product-design scope, without pretending to prove a new hiring trend.

editions.headline: More features are not a stronger product.
editions.summary: When more people can produce credible design work, senior influence can come from shaping a coherent whole. Today’s deeper read separates a useful responsibility from unsupported predictions about job titles.

editions.headline: A title is not a scope agreement.
editions.summary: The useful career question is not whether designers must become something else. It is which decisions they own, what quality they can demonstrate, and how their work helps other teams deliver.

editions.headline: Make the missing evidence visible.
editions.summary: A convincing answer is not the same as a representative one. The useful senior-design move is to show which decisions rest on observation, which rest on assumptions, and what would change your mind.

editions.headline: Design the work behind the interface.
editions.summary: When generating an interface gets easier, the operating experience deserves more attention: who maintains content, who can change it, and how people recover when it goes wrong. That is a concrete senior-level design problem—not a prediction that a job title will disappear.

editions.headline: The next design deliverable is a decision people can test.
editions.summary: Figma’s October 15 releases put working code and written intent beside the canvas. The senior-level opportunity is not producing more artifacts; it is making consequential choices easier to inspect, challenge and carry into production.

editions.headline: The title may stay. The job is moving.
editions.summary: For a senior staff product designer, the useful question is not whether AI will rename the role. It is which decisions, skills and responsibilities employers increasingly expect you to own.
